name: Negative binomial distribution
seoDesc: Negative binomial distribution: work out combinations (n-1, r-1) from the probability of one success. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units…
summary: The Negative binomial distribution calculator returns combinations (n-1, r-1) from the 3 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. Think of it as a shortcut for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Negative binomial distribution calculator work?
sections.html:
The Negative binomial distribution calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports combinations (n-1, r-1) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the probability of one success.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: The formula behind the Negative binomial distribution calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Combinations (n-1, r-1)=(n (number of events) − 1, r (number of successes) − 1)
Probability of Y=n=((probability of one success ^ r (number of successes)) × (1 − probability of one success ^ n (number of events) − r (number of successes)) × (n (number of events) − 1, r (number of successes) − 1))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Negative binomial distribution calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the probability of one success — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Negative binomial distribution calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — n for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Negative binomial distribution calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns combinations (n-1, r-1), derived from the probability of one success. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Negative binomial distribution calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the probability of one success, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Is the Negative binomial distribution calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
